reports.title: A blank reading can be a clue
reports.summary: A known, simple method cut error by 25.0% in one toy setting. The random-missingness check showed its limit.

next_steps.task: Find a real sensor dataset with recorded failures.
next_steps.why: The toy test cannot tell us how common this pattern is.
next_steps.success: We can trace why and when readings go missing.

document.background:
Imagine a sensor that stops reporting when it gets too hot. Filling the blank with its average makes the input look ordinary. But the blank itself may be a warning.

This example uses a known idea: add a yes/no input saying which readings were missing. The data are generated locally. Team meetings and votes are scripted examples.
document.progress:
We compared two simple predictors on separate test data. Both filled gaps using training-set averages. Only one received the extra missing-reading flags.

With overload-related failures, error fell from 1.613 to 1.211: **25.0% lower**. When readings disappeared at random, the flags gave no benefit.

This supports the mechanism in this toy example. It does not establish a new research contribution or a real-world improvement.
document.next_steps:
Find real data that records sensor failures. Check whether the pattern changes over time, and test on a later period. Keep the average-filling baseline.

Rerun the example with `python3 examples/missing-measurements/run.py`. Inspect all per-seed values in `results.json`.

Added the missing-value guide and a paper for comparison.
Proposed testing whether a blank reading can warn us of overload.

Stopped: the sample file used a different column name.
Checked the file and corrected the input-column mapping. Work could continue.
The overload test finished: marking blanks reduced error by 25.0%.
The random-missingness check showed no benefit.
The benefit grew when high readings were more likely to disappear.
The next useful step is to check a real dataset.

experiment.title: Can a blank reading be useful information?
experiment.summary: Marking blank readings reduced error by 25.0% in the overload example.
experiment.purpose: When sensor A is under high load, it is more likely to stop reporting. Can we use that clue?
experiment.prediction: A model told which readings went blank should predict better than one given only filled-in numbers.

figures.title: Blank readings carry a clue
figures.caption: Average root mean squared error over five independent train/test splits. Synthetic data, arbitrary target units. Full per-seed results are included.

experiment.interpretation: In this toy world, a missing reading often means sensor A was high. A yes/no flag lets the model adjust its prediction.
experiment.uncertainty: The rule causing missing readings is deliberately simple and stays the same at test time. This is an illustration of a known method, not evidence of a new discovery or performance on real sensors.
experiment.next_step: Try real data and check what happens when the sensor’s failure pattern changes.
experiment.setup: 4,000 training rows and 2,000 separate test rows per seed; five seeds. Means and model weights are fitted on training data only.
experiment.baseline: Linear prediction after filling each missing value with its training-set mean.
experiment.data: sample.csv contains the first split; run.py generates all five.
experiment.settings: The high-reading missing probability is 0.9; otherwise 0.1. The other sensors go blank independently with probability 0.12.
experiment.measures: Root mean squared prediction error. Extra cost: three binary inputs, seven rather than four fitted coefficients including the intercept.
experiment.budget: CPU only; no model calls or downloads.
experiment.cost: Thirty fits per method across all conditions.

experiment.title: What if readings disappear at random?
experiment.summary: The flags gave no benefit when missing readings carried no clue about the target.
experiment.purpose: Keep the expected missing rate the same, but remove its link to high sensor readings.

figures.title: The random-missingness check
figures.caption: Average root mean squared error over five independent train/test splits. Synthetic data, arbitrary target units. Full per-seed results are included.

experiment.interpretation: The first result depends on an informative failure pattern. Adding inputs alone was not enough to improve predictions.
experiment.uncertainty: Five splits are useful for a demonstration, not a broad claim about all data.
experiment.next_step: Check whether real sensor failures contain a similar clue.
experiment.setup: Same fit, train/test sizes, and seeds. Missingness is independent of sensor values.

experiment.title: When does the clue become useful?
experiment.summary: The benefit grew as high readings became more likely to disappear.
experiment.purpose: Vary the chance that a high sensor reading goes blank.

figures.title: Stronger missingness clue, larger benefit
figures.x_label: Chance a high reading goes blank
figures.caption: Each point averages five held-out tests. Raw per-seed values are in results.json. These lines show averages, not uncertainty intervals.

experiment.interpretation: As more high readings disappear, the filled values become less reliable. Marking blanks recovers part of the lost information.
experiment.uncertainty: Only three failure settings and one simple data-generating rule were tested.
experiment.setup: High-reading missing probabilities of 0.3, 0.6, and 0.9. Other settings are unchanged.

demo_summary.title: From a question to a checked result
demo_summary.text: 25.0% less prediction error in the overload example. No benefit when readings disappeared at random.

record_questions.body: Does this mean extra inputs always improve predictions?

replies.body: No. In the random-missingness check, the flags did not help. Here, they help only because a missing reading tells us something about the hidden sensor value.
